entities.summary:
Arnail François, marquis de Jaucourt (1757–1852), a prominent French aristocrat and statesman, navigated the turbulent political currents of France from the twilight of the Ancien Régime through the French Revolution, the Napoleonic Empire, the Bourbon Restoration, and into the July Monarchy. His exceptionally long and adaptable career, marked by service across ideologically disparate regimes, made him a quintessential figure of political resilience and moderation during an era of profound societal and governmental upheaval. Jaucourt is significant for embodying the pragmatic adaptability required to maintain influence and contribute to governance amidst continuous revolutionary transformations, advocating consistently for constitutional monarchy.

Born into the high nobility, Jaucourt's political journey commenced as a deputy to the Legislative Assembly in 1791, where he aligned with the moderate Feuillants, advocating for a constitutional monarchy. He emigrated during the radical phase of the Revolution but returned under Napoleon Bonaparte, quickly rising through the ranks to become a member of the Tribunate in 1800 and subsequently a senator in 1803, participating in legislative reforms. With the collapse of the Empire, Jaucourt seamlessly transitioned his allegiance to the Bourbon Restoration, serving as a Peer of France from 1814. During Napoleon's brief return in the Hundred Days (1815), he briefly held the critical portfolio of Minister of Marine, before resuming his role as a trusted Minister of State under Louis XVIII and Charles X, where he contributed to diplomatic and legislative efforts to stabilize post-revolutionary France.

entities.summary:
Arnail François, marquis de Jaucourt, born in Paris in 1757, was a prominent French aristocrat and politician whose career spanned the tumultuous transition from the Ancien Régime through the French Revolution, the Napoleonic Empire, and the Bourbon Restoration, enduring until his death in 1852. A consistent advocate for constitutional monarchy and liberal ideals, Jaucourt served in various high-level capacities, reflecting the adaptability and resilience required to navigate nearly seven decades of profound political upheaval in Western Europe. His enduring presence in French statecraft, from the Legislative Assembly of 1791 to the Chamber of Peers under Louis XVIII, underscores his significance as a witness and participant in the fundamental reshaping of French society and governance.

Jaucourt's political journey began as a deputy for Seine-et-Marne to the Legislative Assembly in 1791, where he aligned with the Feuillants, supporting a constitutional monarchy. Imprisoned during the Reign of Terror, he later resumed public life under the Consulate and Empire, becoming a Senator in 1803 and a Count of the Empire in 1808. Crucially, during the First Restoration, Jaucourt played a pivotal role as Minister of State and as an ambassador to Prussia (1814) and Sardinia (1815). He was instrumental in the drafting of the Charter of 1814, a foundational document for the restored monarchy, and later presided over the Chamber of Peers from 1817 to 1823, helping to stabilize the post-Napoleonic political landscape.
